1359.title: Movements, closed
1359.hook: old schools and new movements, each in its own words
1359.howItsDone: Buddhists belong to many schools and movements, from old Chinese and Japanese schools to modern lay and engaged movements, and each explains its practice and teaching in its own words.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zen centers in the West: a row of shoes, a white wall, teachers from Japan, Korea and Vietnam. Your line: far from home.

A traveler crosses a river on a raft he has lashed together from grass and branches. On the far bank he stops. This raft served me well, he thinks. Should I carry it on my head from now on? In the Buddha's parable, told in full on day four twenty, the answer is no: a raft is for crossing, not for carrying. The Buddha said his teaching was like that raft. These last weeks brought a great many rafts, old and new, built in many countries from many kinds of wood.
screen: `A RAFT OF GRASS AND BRANCHES.` → `FOR CROSSING, NOT CARRYING.` → `MANY RAFTS.`

segments.voice: First, the Chinese schools. Tiantai, the Lotus school, with its three truths and its calming and seeing. Huayan, the flower garland, where everything holds everything else, like Fazang's lion, gold in every hair. Second, the Japanese schools. Tendai on the mother mountain. Shingon, the true word, its two mandalas and the letter A. Then Nichiren and the title of the Lotus Sutra, its written mandala, and the many communities that chant it, each speaking for itself. Third, old roots and new branches. Newar Buddhism in Nepal's Kathmandu Valley, with its householder priests. Then movements of recent times: Goenka's ten-day silent courses, the insight movement, Won Buddhism and its circle, Triratna, Navayana with Ambedkar's followers, and Secular Buddhism, with others who disagree. Fourth, practice put to work. Engaged Buddhism, in hard places. Humanistic Buddhism in Taiwan, and its relief volunteers. The family altar. Communities living together. Zen centers far from home. Some of these schools disagree with each other, sometimes sharply, about texts, practice, authority and what awakening is. Each has described itself here in its own words, unranked, and the next block works the same way: starting tomorrow, the schools side by side, what they share and where they really differ, without crowning a winner. In the parable, the teaching is for crossing over. Each movement met here is a different answer to one question: how do people, in this place and time, build something that floats?
screen: `TIANTAI AND HUAYAN.` · `TENDAI, SHINGON, NICHIREN.` · `OLD ROOTS, NEW BRANCHES.` · `PRACTICE PUT TO WORK.` · then, large: `MANY WAYS.`

segments.voice: Picture a slow river and breathe with it, letting the names from these weeks drift past like rafts: Tiantai, Huayan, Tendai, Shingon, Nichiren, Newar, the ten-day course, insight, Won, Triratna, Navayana, secular, engaged, humanistic, relief, the family altar, communities, Zen in the West. Don't hold on to any of them; just notice which one your attention turns toward, a temple, a course, a community you'd like to see for yourself. Let that one stay a moment.
Movements. The schools and communities of Buddhism, old and new, each with its own practice and its own way of explaining itself. Today's word.
Your line: many ways. Every raft is for crossing, not for carrying. See you tomorrow.

1360.title: What all share: the truths
1360.hook: every school teaches the four truths and the eightfold path
1360.howItsDone: Teachers in the Buddhist schools teach the four noble truths and the eightfold path to beginners, and Buddhists chant or recite them, in Pali, Chinese, Tibetan, Japanese, English and other languages.

segments.voice: Yesterday, many rafts, each one for crossing, not for carrying. Your line: many ways.

In Pali, in a monastery in Sri Lanka. In classical Chinese, in a temple in Taipei. In Tibetan, in a dharma hall in the Himalayas. In English, in a Zen center on a rainy evening. Different robes, bells and languages. Yet listen to what the teachers explain to new students, and the same short list keeps surfacing, the one the Buddha is said to have given in his very first teaching. After weeks on the differences, a new block begins: the schools side by side, ranked by no one, starting with what they hold in common.
screen: `PALI, CHINESE, TIBETAN, ENGLISH.` → `THE SAME SHORT LIST.` → `SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: Day four gave these truths with no jargon; now, how the schools hold them. First, where it starts. The discourse called Setting in Motion the Wheel of the Dhamma tells how the Buddha, after his awakening, went to the Deer Park near Benares and spoke to his old companions, a talk tradition counts as his first. Rhys Davids' translation has him name "the noble truth concerning suffering." Three more follow. Second, the four truths. There is suffering, dukkha: the ache, the unsatisfactoriness that runs through life. It has an arising: craving, the thirst that grasps. It has an ending: when craving is let go, the suffering stops. And there is a way to that ending. Third, the way: the noble eightfold path. Right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness and concentration. Not eight steps to climb in order, teachers say, but eight strands of one rope. Fourth, how the schools hold them. Across the schools this course has visited, the four truths and the path turn up again and again. Theravada teaching keeps them close to the center, in the words of the Pali discourses. Mahayana teachers keep them too, and some read them through emptiness: the Heart Sutra, chanted in Mahayana temples, goes so far as to say there is no suffering, no arising, no ending and no path. Its teachers explain this not as throwing the truths away, but as holding even them without grasping. Some Tibetan teachers place the four truths at the beginning of the path, as the ground everything else stands on. Same truths, held in different hands.
screen: `THE DEER PARK, THE FIRST TEACHING.` · `SUFFERING, ARISING, ENDING, WAY.` · `EIGHT STRANDS OF ONE ROPE.` · `SAME TRUTHS, DIFFERENT HANDS.` · then, large: `SHARED BY ALL.`

segments.voice: Let the breath settle, then say the four truths slowly, one on each out-breath: there is suffering; suffering has an arising; suffering has an ending; there is a way. Let the eight strands of the path come to mind one by one, without trying to remember them perfectly. Notice which one feels closest today, speech perhaps, or effort, or mindfulness, and rest there.
What all share. The four noble truths and the eightfold path, taught across the Buddhist schools in their own languages and their own ways. Today's word.
Your line: shared by all. Four truths, eight strands, many languages. Same time tomorrow.

1361.title: What all share: the jewels
1361.hook: every school takes refuge in the Buddha, the dhamma and the sangha
1361.tomorrow: What all share: ethics and practice
1361.howItsDone: Buddhists take refuge in the Buddha, the dhamma and the sangha, reciting the formula three times in Pali, Chinese, Tibetan, Japanese or another language, at ceremonies, and at the start of practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the four truths and the eightfold path: the same truths, held in different hands. Your line: shared by all.

Buddham saranam gacchami. A room full of people says it together, then again, then a third time. In a Thai temple at dawn, a Korean mountain monastery, an ordination in a Tibetan hall, a Zen ceremony in a rented room, the words and the tune change, but the shape stays recognizable: three things, named, as places to go for shelter. Some people describe saying them as the moment they became Buddhist. It's the second thing the schools share.
screen: `BUDDHAM SARANAM GACCHAMI.` → `SAID AGAIN, AND AGAIN.` → `THREE PLACES OF SHELTER.`

segments.voice: You met the three jewels on day two, and the refuges on day one twenty-three; today, side by side. First, the words. Buddham saranam gacchami: to the Buddha for refuge I go. Then the same for the dhamma, the teaching, and the sangha, the community. The old Pali formula then repeats the whole thing a second time, and a third. Second, why refuge. The Dhammapada pictures frightened people running for shelter to mountains, forests and sacred trees, places that can't really protect them. Then it names a refuge it calls safe. In Max Müller's translation, it's the one who "takes refuge with Buddha, the Law, and the Church." Müller's English sounds strange now: Law is his word for dhamma, and Church his word for sangha. Third, why jewels. Buddhists call the three the triple gem, or the three jewels. Tradition explains the name simply: like gems, they're precious, and worth keeping close. Fourth, the schools side by side. Theravada communities recite the refuges in Pali, often followed by the precepts. Zen and other East Asian schools take the refuges in ordination and lay ceremonies, in Chinese, Korean, Japanese or Vietnamese. In Tibetan Buddhism, refuge prayers are said at the start of practice, and some lineages also name the teacher, the lama, alongside the three. Pure Land and Nichiren communities hold the jewels in their own ways too. What the Buddha means, what counts as the teaching, who belongs to the community: the schools answer those differently. But across the schools met so far, the three names come back. Tomorrow, the third thing they share.
screen: `TO THE BUDDHA FOR REFUGE I GO.` · `A SAFE REFUGE.` · `WHY THEY ARE CALLED JEWELS.` · `ONE SHAPE, MANY TONGUES.` · then, large: `THREE JEWELS FOR ALL.`

segments.voice: Sit upright, palms together if that feels right. If you're a Buddhist, or wish to be, say the old words slowly, Buddham saranam gacchami, Dhammam saranam gacchami, Sangham saranam gacchami; if they're not your words, simply listen to them in your mind, as words that hold a whole family of schools together. Then notice, without judging, where you go for shelter when life gets hard: a person, a place, a habit.
What all share. The three jewels, the Buddha, the dhamma and the sangha, in which Buddhists of the schools take refuge. Today's word.
Your line: three jewels for all. Three names that keep on coming back. Until tomorrow.

1362.title: What all share: ethics and practice
1362.hook: precepts, meditation and kindness run through every school
1362.howItsDone: Lay Buddhists in Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana communities often recite the five precepts as training rules they take on, alongside meditation and chanting for the good of all beings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the three jewels: the Buddha, the dhamma and the sangha, the refuge the schools hold in common. Your line was three jewels for all.

Three robes at one breakfast table. Saffron, from a forest monastery in Thailand. Black, from a Zen temple in Japan. Maroon, from a Tibetan nunnery. One chanted the precepts in Pali before dawn. One sat facing a white wall until the bell. One recited verses wishing every being well. Three very different mornings. Listen a little longer, though, and three threads run through all of them: a promise about how to act, a time for training the mind, and a wish for other people's good.
screen: `SAFFRON, BLACK, MAROON.` → `THREE MORNINGS.` → `THE SAME THREE THREADS.`

segments.voice: First, conduct. The Pali word is sila. For lay Buddhists it takes the shape of the five precepts: no killing, no stealing, no sexual misconduct, no false speech, and no intoxicants that cloud the mind. They aren't commandments handed down but training rules a person takes on: I undertake to train in this. Monks and nuns keep far more rules, and some Mahayana communities add bodhisattva precepts on top. But the five are the ground floor. Second, training the mind. Here the schools look very different. Noting the rise and fall of the belly in Burma. Zazen in Japan. Visualizing a Buddha in Tibet. Walking slowly in a Korean courtyard. Chanting a name in a Chinese hall. Underneath runs the same work: steadying attention so it can see clearly. Third, kindness. Theravada homes chant the discourse on loving-kindness, metta. Mahayana temples speak of great compassion, the wish to free all beings. Different words, both wishes for other people's good. Fourth, one verse gathers it all. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, says: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened." A Thai monk, a Japanese priest and a Tibetan nun could each recite their own version of that line, and mean it.
screen: `SILA: PRECEPTS TAKEN ON, NOT IMPOSED.` · `MANY SHAPES OF MEDITATION.` · `METTA AND GREAT COMPASSION.` · `NOT TO HARM, TO DO GOOD, TO PURIFY.` · then, large: `THE COMMON GROUND.`

What all share. Beneath the robes and the languages: precepts, a trained mind and kindness, running underneath the schools we've met this year. Today's word.
Your line: the common ground. Three robes, and one floor beneath all of them. See you tomorrow.

1363.title: Three turnings
1363.hook: a Mahayana map of three turnings of the wheel; other schools map it differently
1363.howItsDone: Tibetan monastic colleges study the three turnings in depth and debate which is definitive, while Theravada teachers keep the Pali canon and its first discourse at the deer park as the turning of the wheel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, what all share: precepts, a trained mind and kindness under every robe. Your line was the common ground.

In a deer park near Benares, the Buddha gives his first teaching to a few old companions who had once walked away from him: the four truths, the middle way. You met that morning back in year one. The Pali text says that when he finished, the cry went up from the earth to the heavens: the wheel of the teaching has been set rolling. The schools took that picture in different directions. Some say the wheel turned once, at the deer park, and has been rolling ever since. Others say it turned again, and then a third time.
screen: `THE DEER PARK.` → `THE WHEEL SET ROLLING.` → `ONCE, OR THREE TIMES?`

segments.voice: First, the deer park itself. In the Pali canon this talk is the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, setting the wheel of dhamma in motion; Rhys Davids gave it a grand English title, The Foundation of the Kingdom of Righteousness. Every map today starts here. Second, the Mahayana map. A Mahayana scripture, the Samdhinirmocana Sutra, describes the teaching turning in three stages. First, the four truths, taught at the deer park. Second, the teaching of emptiness, found in the Perfection of Wisdom sutras. Third, a turning that clarifies the second, carefully distinguishing what is meant literally from what needs interpreting. That map became important in Tibet. Third, maps inside the map. Tibetan schools don't agree on which turning is final. Some hold that the second, on emptiness, is the definitive word; others give that place to the third, and each sets out its reasons in long, careful debate. In China, Tiantai teachers drew a different map again, arranging the sutras into periods of the Buddha's teaching life. Fourth, the Theravada view. The Theravada keeps the Pali canon as the Buddha's word and doesn't accept the later sutras into it. For a Theravada teacher, the wheel set rolling at the deer park is the wheel, still turning, with no second or third. Each map orders a huge body of teaching, and they can lie side by side without one being torn up.
screen: `THE WHEEL SET ROLLING AT THE DEER PARK.` · `A MAHAYANA MAP: THREE TURNINGS.` · `TIBETAN SCHOOLS WEIGH THEM DIFFERENTLY.` · `THERAVADA: ONE WHEEL, STILL TURNING.` · then, large: `MAPS DIFFER.`

1364.title: The arahant ideal
1364.hook: Theravada honors the arahant, fully freed, who also teaches and helps
1364.howItsDone: In Theravada Buddhism the arahant is the goal of the path, and devotees honor the Buddha and his freed disciples with chanting, bows and visits to respected teachers; some Chinese temples keep halls of luohan statues.

segments.voice: Yesterday, three turnings: a Mahayana map of the teaching, and the Theravada's one wheel, still rolling. Your line was maps differ.

A young mother loses everything in one terrible stretch: her children, her husband, her parents. The old commentaries tell how she wandered so lost in grief that her clothes fell away and people drove her off. You may remember her from year one: Patacara. She came to the Buddha, he spoke to her, and over time, the texts say, her mind was freed. Then she taught. The verses of the early nuns, the Therigatha, remember women who came to her in their own grief and found their way. A woman freed, who turned around and helped.
screen: `PATACARA LOSES EVERYTHING.` → `SHE IS FREED.` → `THEN SHE TEACHES.`

segments.voice: First, the word. In Pali, arahant names one who has finished the path: greed, hatred and delusion are gone, and there is no more becoming. In the Theravada it's the goal of practice, for monks and nuns, and in some stories for lay people too. The Buddha himself is called an arahant in the old chant of praise. Second, what it feels like. The Dhammapada has a whole chapter on the arahant, and in Max Müller's translation it opens: "There is no suffering for him who has finished his journey, and abandoned grief, who has freed himself on all sides, and thrown off all fetters." Third, the turning back. The arahant is not a hermit who closes the door. In the Vinaya, the Buddha sends his first freed disciples out on the roads, in the Rhys Davids and Oldenberg translation, "for the gain of the many, for the welfare of the many, out of compassion for the world." Sariputta taught. Patacara taught. In Theravada lands, people still seek out teachers they regard as freed, for a word, a blessing, a way through. Fourth, honored beyond its home. In Chinese temples, halls of arhat statues, the luohan, line the walls: laughing, scratching, sleeping, thinking, each one a freed disciple. The Theravada puts the arahant at the center; other schools honor arahants too, in their own way. Tomorrow, a second ideal.

1365.title: The bodhisattva ideal
1365.hook: the Mahayana honors the bodhisattva who vows to help all; the two ideals are both honored in their own homes
1365.howItsDone: Mahayana Buddhists often take bodhisattva vows and recite them in temples and retreats, and honor bodhisattvas like Guanyin with chanting and offerings; Theravada Buddhists tell the Jataka stories of the Buddha's past lives as a bodhisatta.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the arahant: Patacara, freed after grief, who turned around and taught. Your line was fully freed.

Long before he was the Buddha, the Pali Jataka tales say, he was a hare, a monkey king, a prince who gave away everything he had. Life after life, the stories follow one being on the long road to awakening. The Pali word for him in those lives is bodhisatta, the Buddha-to-be, and the Theravada still tells those stories in temples and at festivals. Then the Mahayana sutras take that word and open the door wide. Not just one Buddha-to-be: anyone can take the vow and walk that road, for the sake of every living being.
screen: `A HARE, A MONKEY KING, A PRINCE.` → `THE BUDDHA-TO-BE.` → `THE DOOR OPENS WIDE.`

segments.voice: First, the vow. In the Mahayana, a bodhisattva sets their heart on full awakening, not for themselves alone but to free all beings. That turning of the heart is called bodhicitta, the mind of awakening. Zen students chant a set of great vows, and the first is to free beings without number. Second, the long patience. The Indian poet-monk Shantideva wrote a line Tibetan teachers often quote: as long as space remains, and as long as beings remain, may I too remain, to ease the sorrows of the world. Some bodhisattvas have temples and festivals of their own. Avalokiteshvara, called Guanyin in China and Kannon in Japan, hears the cries of the world; you met Guanyin in year three. Kshitigarbha, tradition says, vowed not to rest until the hells are empty. Third, the two ideals in their own homes. The Theravada centers the arahant and honors the bodhisatta path of the Buddha himself. The Mahayana centers the bodhisattva and honors the arahants in its temple halls. Each explains its ideal in its own words, and neither needs the other to be smaller. Fourth, the week behind us: what all share, the truths, the jewels, ethics and practice; the three turnings and their different maps; the arahant, fully freed; and now the bodhisattva.
screen: `THE VOW TO FREE ALL BEINGS.` · `AS LONG AS SPACE REMAINS.` · `TWO IDEALS IN THEIR OWN HOMES.` · `THE WEEK: SHARED GROUND, TWO IDEALS.` · then, large: `BOTH HONORED.`

segments.voice: On the in-breath, bring to mind Patacara, freed, turning back to teach; on the out-breath, Guanyin, listening for the cries of the world. Let each be honored as its own home honors it, without weighing one against the other. If one moves you more today, that's fine; keep a little room for the other.
The bodhisattva ideal. One who sets their heart on awakening for the sake of all beings: the Buddha-to-be in the Jatakas, the open vow in the Mahayana. Today's word.
Your line: both honored. Two ideals, two homes, and neither one made smaller. I'll be here tomorrow.

chat.says: Do Theravada Buddhists reject the bodhisattva idea completely?
options: No. They tell the Jataka tales of the bodhisatta, the Buddha-to-be, but center the arahant.
Yes. The word for it only appears in Mahayana texts, never once in the Pali ones.
No. They center the bodhisattva vow too, exactly the way Zen and Tibet do.
chat.meaning: The Pali Jatakas call the Buddha in his former lives the bodhisatta; the Theravada centers the arahant, while the Mahayana opens the bodhisattva vow to all.
